questions.lessonTitle: Augustus and the Origin of the Title Emperor
questions.lessonContent: Octavian became sole ruler of Rome after defeating Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium. The Senate gave him the name "Augustus," meaning "most high." In 23 BCE, he was made consul for life and given several titles including "Imperator," meaning "successful general." This title "Imperator" became the origin of the English word "emperor." questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The quality of emperors who succeeded Augustus varied greatly. Tiberius (14-37 CE) was Augustus's stepson, a capable general who strengthened the empire's northern frontier before retiring to Capri. Caligula (37-41 CE), named for the "little boots" he wore as a child in the army, ruled effectively for two years before suffering a severe illness followed by two years of horrible rule, killing family members and perceived enemies before being assassinated. Claudius (41-54 CE) brought southern Britannia under Roman control, opened the Senate to provincials, and conducted a census in 48 CE. Nero (54-68 CE) was considered a tyrant who murdered his mother, stepbrother, wives, and teacher Seneca, and was accused of setting the Great Fire of Rome in 64 CE.

questions.lessonContent: Emperor Diocletian was the first Roman emperor in 100 years to properly restore order after a century of chaos known as the Crisis of the Third Century. questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall and Lasting Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonContent:
Why is ancient Rome so important to world history?

• Administration of a vast empire
• Christianity
• Architecture
• Engineering
• Historians
• Jewish Diaspora
• Literature
• Roman law
• Romance languages
• Transmission of Greek (Hellenistic) culture

The Romans did not necessarily create and invent everything that they are commonly given credit for. What the Romans were best at was taking something (like the Etruscan arch), adapting it, and putting it to great use (such as in the construction of aqueducts).

Administration of a Vast Empire
• Empire included over 100,000,000 people of diverse backgrounds, cultures, and places
• Rome learned to adapt its policies on a local level to fit the people of a given area
• Citizenship gradually extended to all free men of the empire
• Solid, strong bureaucracy that kept things running smoothly the majority of the time

Christianity
• Christianity started in the Roman province of Judea
• Pax Romana and Roman infrastructure allowed early Christians to travel freely throughout the empire
• Christianity finally gained acceptance with the Edict of Milan (313 CE) and Constantine's conversion

Architecture & Engineering
• A large part of Rome's success was due to the importance Rome placed on building and maintaining the empire's infrastructure
• Aqueducts, bridges, dams, harbors, roads
• Public buildings including amphitheaters, basilicas, government offices, palaces, public baths, theaters

Historians
• Julius Caesar - Commentaries on the Gallic Wars
• Cicero - Letters and orations, called the "Father of Latin prose"
• Livy - Annals, history of Rome from beginnings to Augustus
• Plutarch - Parallel Lives, comparison of Greek and Roman heroes
• Tacitus - Germania, Annals and Histories

Jewish Diaspora
• The Romans put down a series of uprisings in Judea-Palestina
• After the Bar Kokhba Revolt (132-136 BCE), the Jews were forced to migrate from the area around Jerusalem

Roman Law
• Started with the Twelve Tables (450 BCE)
• Developed over a thousand years including decisions of judges, ideas of the Republic and Empire, and rulings of emperors
• Justinian Code (6th century CE) encapsulated the previous 1000+ years of Roman law
• Still used as the basis of civil law in many parts of Europe

Romance Languages
• Romance languages developed from Latin: French, Italian, Portuguese, Romanian, Spanish
• The Catholic Church preserved the Latin language
• Catholic masses were said in Latin until the 1960s

questions.lessonTitle: Factors Contributing to the Fall of the Western Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Western Roman Empire began its decline primarily due to economic decline, where the widening gap between rich and poor reduced purchasing power and harmed trade. The combination of economic and military crises then produced political instability, with frequent changes of emperor, civil wars, and an inability to govern effectively. questions.lessonContent: A multi-agent research system uses multiple autonomous agents that work together to explore complex topics. Our Research system specifically employs an orchestrator-worker pattern where a lead agent coordinates the research process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. This means that whenever deploying updates, agents might be anywhere in their process. We therefore need to prevent our well-meaning code changes from breaking existing agents. We cannot update every agent to the new version at the same time. questions.lessonContent: Software engineering agents aim to autonomously act to solve a given task prompt. Given an environment, which includes a codebase and an isolated container for code execution, along with a prompt giving the agent its task, an agent produces a rollout consisting of a series of actions. Each action makes one or more tool calls and yields responses, and tool calls may modify the underlying environment. The result of a rollout is the final state of this environment. Each action is selected by sampling from a language model policy, after which a reward is given based on the code's correctness, succinctness, and conformance to software engineering principles. Unlike more constrained settings like competitive programming, a strong software engineering agent must perform non-trivial exploration, write its own tests, and construct the minimal changes necessary to solve the task prompt.

questions.lessonContent: PNG supports several prediction methods that attempt to predict each pixel based on its neighbors. questions.lessonTitle: Lossless Compression Achievements for Different Image Types
questions.lessonContent: Lossless compression like PNG preserves every single pixel while still shrinking the file size. The actual compression ratio achieved depends heavily on the type of image being compressed. For photographs with continuous tones and complex patterns, the compression is more modest because there are fewer repeated patterns to exploit. For screenshots with large solid color regions and sharp edges, compression is dramatically more effective because adjacent pixels are very similar and patterns repeat frequently. PNG combines three techniques: filtering to store differences, LZ77 to find patterns, and Huffman coding for efficient bit representation.

questions.lessonTitle: Defining Multi-Agent Systems in Research Contexts
questions.lessonContent: A multi-agent system consists of multiple agents, defined as LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop, working together to accomplish complex tasks. The Research feature involves an agent that plans a research process based on user queries and then uses tools to create parallel agents that search for information simultaneously. These systems introduce new challenges in agent coordination, evaluation, and reliability compared to single-agent systems. The architecture enables thorough, independent investigations through subagents that operate with separation of concerns—distinct tools, prompts, and exploration trajectories. This separation reduces path dependency and allows agents to explore different aspects of a question before condensing the most important tokens for the lead research agent.

questions.lessonTitle: Token Usage Differences in Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Multi-agent systems scale performance through distributed work across agents with separate context windows, enabling parallel reasoning. In their analysis, three factors explained 95% of the performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation: token usage explained 80% of the variance, with the number of tool calls and model choice as the other two factors. This validates the architecture that adds capacity for parallel reasoning. However, there is a significant downside: in practice, these architectures burn through tokens fast. Specifically, agents typically use about 4 times more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15 times more tokens than chats. For economic viability, multi-agent systems require tasks where the value of the task is high enough to pay for the increased performance.

questions.moduleTitle: Foundations and Architecture of Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: The Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. The workflow involves a LeadResearcher agent that creates specialized Subagents with specific research tasks, where each subagent independently performs web searches, evaluates tool results using interleaved thinking, and returns findings to the LeadResearcher. The LeadResearcher synthesizes these results and decides whether more research is needed. Once sufficient information is gathered, the system passes all findings to a CitationAgent, which processes the documents and research report to identify specific locations for citations. This ensures all claims are properly attributed to their sources before the final research results are returned to the user.

questions.lessonTitle: Prompt Engineering Principles for Multi-Agent Research
questions.lessonContent: The Anthropic team developed eight key principles for prompting research agents. questions.lessonTitle: Understanding Digital Images and Pixel Structure
questions.lessonContent: Images appear smooth and continuous but are actually composed of tiny colored squares called pixels. Each pixel contains three numerical values representing the amount of red, green, and blue to mix together, with each value ranging from 0 (representing none) to 255 (representing maximum intensity). For example, the color orange is expressed as rgb(255, 147, 41), indicating maximum red, moderate green, and low blue. A standard HD screenshot with dimensions of 1920 × 1080 pixels contains over 2 million pixels, and since each pixel requires 3 bytes (one each for red, green, and blue), an uncompressed single image would be approximately 6.2 megabytes. This basic understanding of pixel structure explains why compression is essential for managing image file sizes.

questions.lessonTitle: The Role of Lossy Compression in Image Processing
questions.lessonContent: Lossy compression is one of two fundamental approaches to image compression and works by intentionally discarding data that humans are unlikely to notice. This technique exploits specific characteristics of human vision: our eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but tend to blur color information together, meaning we notice blurry edges but not slight color variations. JPEG, the primary format using lossy compression, employs several key steps: it first converts pixels from RGB to a different format that separates brightness from color, then reduces color resolution since our eyes won't detect this loss. The image is divided into 8×8 pixel blocks, and each block is transformed into frequency components where low frequencies represent smooth gradients and high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges. Since photographs primarily consist of smooth gradients, most information resides in just a few low-frequency components, allowing the high-frequency details to be discarded without noticeable quality loss.

questions.lessonTitle: Lossless Compression Techniques: Filtering, Pattern Finding, and Encoding
questions.lessonContent: Lossless compression preserves every single pixel perfectly while still reducing file size through three key techniques. The first technique, called filtering or prediction, leverages the fact that adjacent pixels are usually similar; instead of storing each value directly, the algorithm stores how much each pixel differs from its neighbor, with PNG supporting methods including Sub (predict from left), Up (predict from above), Average, and Paeth. The second technique uses the LZ77 algorithm to identify repeated patterns in the data, replacing sequences with back-references that point back to previous occurrences within a sliding window of the last 32 KB. The third technique applies Huffman coding, which assigns shorter binary codes to more frequently occurring values—for instance, a value appearing 60% of the time might receive just 1 bit while rarer values receive longer codes. PNG combines all three tricks in sequence: filtering first, then LZ77 pattern-finding, then Huffman encoding, before wrapping everything in the PNG file format with headers and checksums.

questions.lessonTitle: The Orchestrator-Worker Pattern in Multi-Agent Research
questions.lessonContent: Our Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. The subagents act as intelligent filters by iteratively using search tools to gather information and then returning findings to the lead agent so it can compile a final answer. After synthesis, the system passes all findings to a CitationAgent which processes documents to identify specific locations for citations.

questions.lessonTitle: Parallel Tool Calling Improves Research Speed
questions.lessonContent: Our multi-agent system introduces two kinds of parallelization to improve speed: first, the lead agent spins up 3-5 subagents in parallel rather than serially; second, the subagents themselves use 3 or more tools in parallel. These changes cut research time by up to 90% for complex queries, allowing Research to do more work in minutes instead of hours while covering more information than other systems. Complex research tasks naturally involve exploring many sources, and early agents that executed sequential searches were painfully slow.

questions.lessonTitle: Scaling Effort Based on Query Complexity
questions.lessonContent: Agents struggle to judge appropriate effort for different tasks, so we embedded scaling rules in the prompts. Simple fact-finding requires just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each, and complex research might use more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities. These explicit guidelines help the lead agent allocate resources efficiently and prevent overinvestment in simple queries, which was a common failure mode in early versions.

questions.lessonContent: When engineering prompts for multi-agent research systems, a specific sequence of principles proves most effective. First, engineers must build an accurate mental model of how agents operate by running simulations and observing behavior step-by-step. Second, they create a delegation framework that teaches the lead agent how to decompose queries into subtasks with clear objectives and task boundaries. Third, they add parallel tool calling to enable both lead agents to spawn multiple subagents simultaneously and subagents to use multiple tools at once, dramatically improving research speed.

questions.lessonTitle: Context Window Limits in Multi-Agent Research
questions.lessonContent: Production agents engage in conversations spanning hundreds of turns, requiring careful context management strategies. As conversations extend, standard context windows become insufficient, necessitating intelligent compression and memory mechanisms. The Research system implements patterns where agents summarize completed work phases and store essential information in external memory before proceeding to new tasks. When context limits approach, agents can spawn fresh subagents with clean contexts while maintaining continuity through careful handoffs. Specifically, if the context window exceeds 200,000 tokens it will be truncated, making it important for the lead agent to save its plan to Memory to persist the context.

questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. This creates unique challenges during deployment because whenever updates are deployed, agents might be anywhere in their process. Anthropic needs to prevent well-meaning code changes from breaking existing agents that are mid-execution. They cannot update every agent to the new version at the same time. Instead, they use rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents, which involves gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously.

questions.lessonContent: In Composer 2's RL infrastructure, the training cluster synchronizes updated model weights to the inference engine via a shared S3 bucket. To minimize transfer size, delta compression is applied where each rank caches its previous upload and transmits only the diff against new weights. The upload is fully sharded across all training ranks to saturate egress bandwidth, while on the inference side, downloads are sharded across inference replicas. Compression, upload, and hotload signaling are pipelined in background workers so that training is never blocked.

questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. questions.lessonContent: PNG files wrap all compressed data in a structured chunk-based format. Each chunk serves a specific purpose: IHDR contains image metadata like width, height, and color type; IDAT holds the actual compressed image data; and IEND marks the end of the file. A critical feature of PNG is its use of checksums for data integrity. Each chunk includes a CRC-32 checksum, which is a mathematical fingerprint of the chunk's data. questions.lessonTitle: KL Divergence Estimator in RL Training
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2's reinforcement learning pipeline uses Kullback-Leibler divergence for regularization between the policy and reference models. Many open-source implementations use the k3 estimator, which is unbiased and reduces variance when the distributions are close. However, research shows that variance increases drastically as the distributions diverge, making k3 problematic for large KL values. The k2 estimator does not suffer from variance blow-up but is biased. To balance these concerns, Composer 2 uses the standard k1 estimator instead, which provides more stable training behavior.

questions.lessonContent: After filtering and pattern-finding, PNG uses Huffman coding to assign shorter binary codes to more frequently occurring values. The most common value (0, appearing 60% of the time) receives just 1 bit. Values appearing 25% of the time get 2 bits, while rarer values appearing 10% or 5% of the time receive 3 bits each. questions.lessonTitle: Definition and Core Benefits of Multi-Agent Research Systems
questions.lessonContent: A multi-agent research system consists of multiple agents, defined as LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop, working together to accomplish complex tasks. Research work involves open-ended problems where it is very difficult to predict the required steps in advance, making AI agents particularly well-suited for these tasks due to their flexibility to pivot or explore tangential connections as investigations unfold. Subagents facilitate compression by operating in parallel with their own context windows, exploring different aspects of a question simultaneously before condensing the most important tokens for the lead research agent. Each subagent also provides separation of concerns—distinct tools, prompts, and exploration trajectories—which reduces path dependency and enables thorough, independent investigations.

questions.lessonContent: In agentic systems, minor changes cascade into large behavioral changes, making it difficult to write code for complex agents that must maintain state in long-running processes. questions.lessonContent: Multi-agent systems don't work like traditional AI evaluations where given input X, the system follows path Y to produce output Z. questions.lessonTitle: KL Divergence Estimator Selection for RL Training
questions.lessonContent: For regularization, Composer 2 uses Kullback-Leibler divergence expressed as KL(q||p) = Ex∼q[−log r(x)] where r(x) = p(x)/q(x). Many open-source RL implementations estimate KL using the k3 estimator defined as (r −1) −log r, which is unbiased and reduces variance when distributions are close. However, research shows that variance increases drastically as p and q diverge. The k2 estimator does not suffer from variance blow-up but is biased. Composer 2 uses the standard k1 estimator instead, which provides more stable gradient estimates when KL values become large during training.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG uses several clever techniques to reduce file size. First, it converts pixels from RGB to a different format that separates brightness from color, reducing color resolution since our eyes won't notice. Then it divides the image into 8x8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components. Since photographs are mostly smooth gradients, most information ends up in just a few low-frequency components, allowing JPEG to throw away high-frequency details.

This simplifies coordination but creates bottlenecks in information flow between agents. The lead agent cannot steer subagents in real time, subagents cannot coordinate with each other, and the entire system can be blocked while waiting for a single subagent to finish searching. Asynchronous execution would enable additional parallelism where agents work concurrently and create new subagents when needed.

questions.lessonContent: Research outputs are difficult to evaluate programmatically since they are free-form text and rarely have a single correct answer. LLMs are a natural fit for grading outputs. Anthropic used an LLM judge that evaluated each output against criteria in a rubric: factual accuracy (do claims match sources?), citation accuracy (do the cited sources match the claims?), completeness (are all requested aspects covered?), source quality (did it use primary sources over lower-quality secondary sources?), and tool efficiency (did it use the right tools a reasonable number of times?). They experimented with multiple judges to evaluate each component but found that a single LLM call with a single prompt outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade was the most consistent and aligned with human judgements.

questions.lessonContent: Agent-tool interfaces are as critical as human-computer interfaces. Using the right tool is efficient—often it is strictly necessary. For instance, an agent searching the web for context that only exists in Slack is doomed from the start. With MCP servers that give the model access to external tools, this problem compounds as agents encounter unseen tools with descriptions of wildly varying quality. Anthropic gave their agents explicit heuristics: examine all available tools first, match tool usage to user intent, search the web for broad external exploration, or prefer specialized tools over generic ones. Simple fact-finding requires just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each, and complex research might use more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities. Without these scaling rules, agents would spawn 50 subagents for simple queries or scour the web endlessly for nonexistent sources.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 trains additional Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) layers to serve the model faster in production for speculative decoding. The MTP layers are initialized from scratch and trained on the same data mix as the main model. To speed up convergence, the MTP layers are trained with self-distillation, which teaches the model to predict the exact logit distribution of the main LM head at each position. Importantly, the MTP layers are trained atop a checkpoint cut from the middle of the continued pretraining run rather than the final checkpoint. During the final two phases of continued pretraining (long-context extension and SFT), the MTP layers are included and trained jointly with the rest of the model.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses the self-summarization technique to enable the model to work across long horizons. Each training rollout can involve multiple generations chained together by summaries, rather than a single prompt-response pair. The final reward is used for all tokens produced by the model in the chain, which upweights both the agent responses in good trajectories and also the self-summarizations that made them work. Poor summaries that lose critical information are downweighted. As Composer trains, it learns to use self-summaries to process more information, even with a limited context window. For hard examples, it often self-summarizes multiple times.

questions.lessonContent: Many open-source implementations of RL estimate KL with the estimator k3 = (r -1) - log r, which is an unbiased estimator of KL and reduces variance when p and q are close. However, research shows that variance increases drastically as p and q diverge, making k3 problematic for large KL values. The k2 estimator does not suffer from variance blow-up but is biased. The k1 estimator is defined as -log r. Composer 2 uses the standard estimator k1 = -log r instead of k3 because k1 avoids the extreme variance issues that k3 exhibits when the KL divergence becomes large.

questions.lessonContent: The Latin phrase "primus inter pares" means "first among equals" and describes how Augustus and later emperors attempted to maintain the facade that they were elected officials rather than dictators. Being "first among equals" gave the illusion that an emperor was the most prestigious and important member of the Roman Senate, while simultaneously suggesting that each senator was equally important. In reality, Roman emperors ruled with little input from anyone else, despite the ceremonial pretense of shared power.

questions.lessonContent: Anthropic's Research system originally used synchronous execution where the lead agent waits for each set of subagents to complete before proceeding. This created bottlenecks in information flow because the lead agent cannot steer subagents, subagents cannot coordinate with each other, and the entire system can be blocked while waiting for a single subagent. They introduced two kinds of parallelization: the lead agent spins up 3-5 subagents in parallel rather than serially, and subagents use 3+ tools in parallel. These changes cut research time by up to 90% for complex queries.

questions.lessonTitle: KL Divergence Estimator for RL Regularization
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence for regularization during reinforcement learning, calculated as KL(q||p) = Ex~q[-log r(x)] where r(x) = p(x)/q(x). While many open-source implementations use the k3 estimator which is unbiased but suffers from drastically increased variance when p and q diverge, the Composer 2 team uses the standard k1 estimator instead (-log r). This choice was made because for large KL values, the variance of the k3 estimate becomes extremely large, making k1 more stable.

questions.lessonContent: Since Kimi K2.5 is a Mixture-of-Experts model, numerical differences can cause different experts to be chosen in the inference engine forward pass and trainer forward pass. To address this, the team employs router replay: during inference, the engine returns the selected expert indices for every token at every MoE layer, and during the training forward pass the router's expert assignment is overridden to match. The router still computes gating scores so that gradients flow through it. This ensures that log-probabilities computed during training match the distribution from which tokens were sampled, preventing noise in the policy gradient. The scheme was extended by filtering out replayed experts whose gating scores fall below a plausibility threshold derived from the router's own top-k selections.

questions.lessonTitle: LLM Judge Evaluation Criteria for Research Agents

questions.lessonContent: Evaluating agents that modify persistent state across multi-turn conversations presents unique challenges. questions.lessonTitle: Scaling Subagent Resources by Query Complexity
questions.lessonContent: When designing prompts for multi-agent research systems, it is essential to embed scaling rules that help the lead agent allocate appropriate resources for different task complexities. Simple fact-finding queries require just one subagent with three to ten tool calls, as these tasks need minimal exploration. Direct comparison tasks typically need two to four subagents with ten to fifteen tool calls each, as they require evaluating multiple sources in parallel. Complex research tasks that involve investigating multiple independent directions may require more than ten subagents with clearly divided responsibilities, ensuring thorough coverage of each aspect. Without these explicit guidelines embedded in prompts, agents tend to overinvest resources on simple queries, which was a common failure mode in early versions of such systems.

questions.lessonContent: In traditional software, a bug might break a feature, degrade performance, or cause outages. In agentic systems, minor changes cascade into large behavioral changes. Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. This means that whenever deploy updates, agents might be anywhere in their process. We therefore need to prevent well-meaning code changes from breaking existing agents. We cannot update every agent to the new version at the same time. Instead, we use rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents, by gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously.

questions.lessonContent: Software engineering agents aim to autonomously act to solve a given task prompt. Given an environment, i.e., a codebase and an isolated container for code execution, along with a prompt giving the agent its task, an agent produces a rollout consisting of a series of actions, each of which makes one or more tool calls and yields responses. Tool calls may modify the underlying environment, and the result of a rollout is the final state of this environment. Each action is selected by sampling from a language model policy, after which a reward is given based on the code's correctness, succinctness, and conformance to software engineering principles. In contrast to more constrained settings like competitive programming, a strong software engineering agent must perform non-trivial exploration, write its own tests, and construct the minimal changes necessary to solve the task prompt.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses Context Parallelism (CP) as the primary long-context scaling axis, which requires less communication than Tensor Parallelism and improves compute efficiency by preserving full hidden dimensions in various projections. The implementation includes several key techniques: computing local KV latent vectors and all-gathering them across CP ranks before computing KV projections to minimize communication overhead. Additionally, the sequence is split into 2 × CP chunks to address load imbalance during causal attention, with the i-th rank processing chunks i and 2 × CP −1 −i, resulting in roughly equal work during causal attention for all ranks. The context parallelism dimension is folded into the FSDP dimension, allowing CP ranks to reduce per-GPU parameter and state memory usage. Composer 2 uses EP=8, CP=2 for continued pretraining and EP=8, CP=8 for the RL phase.

questions.lessonTitle: NVFP4 Quantization Format for MoE Forward Pass
questions.lessonContent: For the MoE forward pass, Composer 2 uses a novel variant of NVFP4 where values are quantized from BF16 into FP4E2M1 using FP8E4M3 per-block scales with block size 16 and FP32 per-token scales. The original NVFP4 format used FP32 per-tensor scales but was found to be fragile for two reasons: per-tensor scaling makes training batch-variant, collapsing numerical precision and causing RL training to diverge, and inter-token scale values leak future token information into past tokens, resulting in biased gradients. Despite adding latency to quantization and GEMM epilogue, per-token scaling proved more effective. The backward pass uses the standard MXFP8 format with FP8E4M3 values and FP8E8M0 scales per 32-element block, providing higher precision to improve training stability since backward pass runs only on the training cluster.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2's continued pretraining stage is divided into three distinct phases. The first and most compute-intensive phase trains at a 32k token sequence length. This is followed by a shorter long-context extension phase that extends the sequence length to 256k tokens. Finally, a brief supervised fine-tuning phase focuses on targeted coding tasks. The training was performed using MXFP8 precision on NVIDIA B300s GPUs with the AdamW optimizer. Additionally, Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) layers were trained alongside the main model to enable faster speculative decoding in production.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 employs self-summarization to handle long-horizon tasks across extended contexts. Each training rollout can involve multiple generations chained together by summaries rather than being limited to a single prompt-response pair. The final reward is applied to all tokens produced by the model in the chain, which upweights both successful agent responses and the self-summarizations that enabled them. Poor summaries that lose critical information are downweighted. As Composer trains, it learns to use self-summaries to process more information even within a limited context window, often self-summarizing multiple times for difficult examples.

questions.lessonTitle: Nonlinear Length Penalty for Task Difficulty
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses a concave down and increasing nonlinear length penalty to incentivize efficient behavior. The formula is Clength{k,q}(x) = ((1 + kx)^(1-q) - 1) / (k(1-q)), where k and q are hyperparameters defining curvature, and x is a weighted combination of thinking tokens, tool calling tokens, tool output tokens, final message tokens, number of tool calls, and number of turns. This nonlinearity reflects that on easy tasks achievable with few tool calls, every additional effort is felt more acutely than in long-horizon tasks where an agent might iterate for hundreds of tool calls. The model learns to be quick on easy tasks while thinking longer on hard requests.

questions.lessonContent: CursorBench evaluation goes beyond functional correctness to assess multiple dimensions of coding agent quality.
